doc.title: John LaPorta interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 13, 1996

title: Classical clarinet study and the 1957 Brahms Sonata album
summary: He studied with Gigliotti, chose jazz over a classical career, and recorded a Brahms Sonata album for Fantasy that bombed but that Hentoff's liner notes predicted would find an audience.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: When you grew up you were into classical technique first?
Well I started that way, yeah. I studied with Joseph Gigliotti in Philadelphia and his son has been for quite a few years the first clarinetist with the Philadelphia Orchestra.
Did you have aspirations as a classical clarinetist?

Well I did then, and I got more and more involved with the jazz end of it, and it seemed just too difficult for me to try to keep up both things, especially at that time. Because Wynton Marsalis made a liar out of me you know, because he’s done beautifully at both of them. I did record the Brahms Sonata for Clarinet, that was quite a few years ago. I was under exclusive contract with Fantasy and I thought one of my projects each year would be to do a serious work, by serious I mean classical work, and then do something on the other side that was comparable to it as a jazz venue. And the first effort that I did was the Brahms Sonata in F and on the other side I had like a Benny Goodman type trio. And it’s a wonderful album but it bombed. The classical critics then wouldn’t handle it, and the jazz critics then couldn’t. But there was something prophetic in the liner notes that Nat Hentoff wrote, he wrote that, he says this is the kind of album that in 1984 would probably reach an audience. And 1984 was the year that Wynton Marsalis got a double Grammy. Isn’t that wild?
I guess people couldn’t handle both.
It was so prophetic, I couldn’t get over this.
